about: The priest asks God to look favorably upon the offering and accept it, as He accepted the gifts of the just Abel, the sacrifice of Abraham, and what Melchisedech offered to Him. Genesis calls Melchisedech a priest of God most high, and it is the Canon that calls him a high priest.

s01.narrative: The priest spreads his hands and goes on.

s02.translation: Be pleased to look upon these offerings with a serene and kindly countenance, and to accept them, as once You were pleased to accept the gifts of Your servant Abel the just, and the sacrifice of Abraham, our father in faith:

s03.translation: and the offering of Your high priest Melchisedech, a holy sacrifice, a spotless victim.

w002.function: A relative pronoun referring to the offerings named in the preceding prayer.

w003.function: Together with “seréno” (w005), it modifies “vultu” (w006): with a gracious and serene countenance.

w011.function: In the phrase “accépta habére”: “to regard as accepted”.

w015.function: The perfect participle of the deponent verb “dignor”. With “es” (w016), it forms the perfect tense.

w020.note: The adjective may belong to púeri, Thy just servant, or to the name Abel itself. Both readings stand in the translation tradition. This edition attaches it to the name.

w021.function: An indeclinable name: only “púeri” (w018), which it stands in apposition to, shows the genitive.

w026.function: The one of the three names Latin declines: Ábraham, Ábrahæ.

w028.function: A relative pronoun without an expressed antecedent: “that which he offered”. Two appositions follow it.

w031.function: It modifies “sacérdos” (w032). In Genesis 14:18 Melchisedech is called “sacérdos Dei altíssimi” — “priest of God most high”.

w034.function: An indeclinable name, nominative in apposition to “sacérdos” (w032). Melchisedech is the subject of “óbtulit” (w030). Genesis 14:18 says that he brought out bread and wine.

w036.function: The first apposition to “quod” (w028): “a holy sacrifice”.

w038.function: The second apposition to “quod” (w028). Feminine “hóstiam” and neuter “quod” share the accusative case.
